about: Math-to-Lean study lessons (sets A and B), after two independent verification passes and every 'fix' correction applied. Each lesson pairs a math statement with a real declaration of research/kickoff/05-lean-sketch/Fw/Spec. Checked by docs/plan/tools/check-lean-lessons.mjs --check; rendered by docs/plan/math-to-lean.html.

lessons.title: A definition is a function: tick
lessons.why: Every Lean statement in this project talks about functions defined with `def`. Reading one `def` well (name, typed arguments, return type, body) is the first step to reading any theorem.
lessons.english: tick(dt) is the number of 120 Hz ticks in a frame of dt microseconds, rounded to the nearest tick with halves rounded up, computed with whole numbers only.

pairs.note: `def` gives a name to a function. Because the file is inside `namespace Fw.Frames`, the full name is `Fw.Frames.tick`.

An argument, called a binder, written as (name : type). The type `Nat` is ℕ, the numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. The symbol ℕ itself only exists with Mathlib, which this project does not use, so the project writes `Nat`.
The type after the last binder is the result type. Together, `#check @tick` prints `Nat → Nat`, which is the math signature tick: ℕ → ℕ.
`:=` means "is defined as". A plain `=` is a statement that has to be proved.
Multiplication must be written with `*`. Putting two things side by side means function application in Lean: `f x` is f(x), so `240 dt` would try to apply 240 as a function.
A numeric literal. `10^6` would also work, and so would `1_000_000` (underscores are allowed as digit separators).
On `Nat`, `/` is floor division, so ⌊·⌋ comes for free. To round to the nearest tick with halves up, you add half the divisor (10^6 = 2·10^6 / 2) before dividing.
Function application needs no parentheses: tick(4167) is written `tick 4167`. The file checks the edge cases with `#guard tick 0 == 0 && tick 4166 == 0 && tick 4167 == 1` (Frames.lean:22).

lessons.gotcha: `/` on ℕ floors, and division by zero is defined to be 0: `(7 : Nat) / 2 = 3` and `(7 : Nat) / 0 = 0`. So you cannot write the second form dt/8333.3 + 1/2 directly; in ℕ, 1/2 is 0. The trick is to multiply through first and floor-divide once at the end.

exercise.prompt: Translate into a Lean def: for n ∈ ℕ, roundHalf(n) = ⌊(n+1)/2⌋, which is n/2 rounded half up. Then: what is `(7 : Nat) / 0` in Lean?
exercise.answer: `def roundHalf (n : Nat) : Nat := (n + 1) / 2`, and `(7 : Nat) / 0 = 0`. Both are checked in StudyA.lean by `#guard roundHalf 0 == 0 && roundHalf 1 == 1 && roundHalf 2 == 1 && roundHalf 3 == 2` and `theorem nat_div_facts : (7 : Nat) / 2 = 3 ∧ (7 : Nat) / 0 = 0 := by decide`.

lessons.title: For all, and implies: tick_mono
lessons.why: Most theorems in the project have the shape "for all inputs, if these hypotheses hold then this conclusion holds". This lesson shows where ∀ and ⇒ go in Lean, and why some arguments are in braces.
lessons.english: A longer frame never gets a smaller tick count.
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem tick_mono {a b : Nat} (h : a ≤ b) : tick a ≤ tick b := by
  unfold tick; exact Nat.div_le_div_right (by omega)

pairs.note: `theorem` names a statement together with its proof. The name is how you cite the result later.

Binders written before the colon are universally quantified. Braces make the arguments implicit: a caller writes `tick_mono h`, and Lean works out a and b from the type of h. `#check @tick_mono` prints `∀ {a b : Nat}, ...`.
The hypothesis is an argument with its own name, h. In Lean a proof of a ≤ b is a value, and the theorem takes it as input.
Taking the argument (h : A) and returning B is the same as stating A → B. `#check` shows it as `a ≤ b → tick a ≤ tick b`. You could also write `(a b : Nat) : a ≤ b → tick a ≤ tick b`.
Type `\le`. The result `a ≤ b` is a Prop, a statement that can be true or false, not a Bool.
After the final colon comes the conclusion, which is what you must prove.
`by` opens tactic mode. In tactic mode each command changes the goal that is left to prove, much like the sentences of a written proof.

proof_steps.math: Unfolding the definition, we must show ⌊(240a + 10^6)/(2·10^6)⌋ ≤ ⌊(240b + 10^6)/(2·10^6)⌋.
proof_steps.note: `unfold` replaces the name `tick` with its body in the goal. Nothing is proved yet; only the goal is rewritten.

proof_steps.math: Floor division by a fixed number preserves ≤, so it is enough that 240a + 10^6 ≤ 240b + 10^6, and this follows from a ≤ b.
proof_steps.note: The library lemma `Nat.div_le_div_right : a ≤ b → a / c ≤ b / c` closes the goal once it gets a proof of the numerator inequality. The inner `by omega` supplies that proof: omega is a decision procedure for linear arithmetic, and it uses h from the context.

lessons.gotcha: Notice ≤ and not <. The strict version is false, because rounding merges nearby frames: 0 < 4166 but tick 0 = tick 4166 = 0. StudyA.lean proves `¬ (∀ a b : Nat, a < b → tick a < tick b)` (tick_not_strict_mono). If a statement uses strict inequality where the math needs ≤, it is a different theorem, and often a false one.

exercise.prompt: Which Lean states ∀ a, b ∈ ℕ: a ≤ b ⇒ 2a ≤ 2b?  (A) `theorem t (a b : Nat) : a ≤ b → 2 * a ≤ 2 * b`  (B) `theorem t {a b : Nat} (h : a ≤ b) : 2 * a ≤ 2 * b`  (C) `theorem t (a b : Nat) : a ≤ b ∧ 2 * a ≤ 2 * b`
exercise.answer: A and B are both correct and state the same thing. They differ only in packaging: explicit versus implicit arguments, and an arrow versus a named hypothesis. C is wrong because ∧ claims that a ≤ b holds for every pair, which already fails at a = 1, b = 0. StudyA.lean proves double_mono_A, double_mono_B, derives each from the other, and proves double_wrong_C : ¬ (∀ a b : Nat, a ≤ b ∧ 2 * a ≤ 2 * b).

lessons.title: If and only if: tick_ge5_iff
lessons.why: The project turns millisecond thresholds into tick thresholds. An iff states that the two ways of drawing the line pick out exactly the same frames, with nothing gained or lost at the boundary.
lessons.english: A frame is at least 5 ticks long exactly when it lasts at least 37.5 ms (37 500 µs).
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem tick_ge5_iff (dt : Nat) : 5 ≤ tick dt ↔ 37500 ≤ dt := by
  unfold tick; constructor <;> intro h <;> omega

pairs.note: This time the argument is explicit, in parentheses. You call `tick_ge5_iff 40000`, because nothing else in the statement would tell Lean which dt you mean.
The numeral 5 is read as a Nat because `tick dt` is a Nat. Lean finds the type of a numeral from its surroundings.
Type `\iff`. A proof of A ↔ B is a pair of implications: `.mp : A → B` and `.mpr : B → A`.
Write no thin space inside the number. `37_500` is also accepted.
For a goal A ↔ B, `constructor` creates the two subgoals A → B and B → A, just as you prove an iff on paper by doing both directions.
How you use the theorem later. In StudyA.lean, `(tick_ge5_iff 40000).mpr (by decide) : 5 ≤ tick 40000`.

proof_steps.note: This replaces `tick dt` with its formula, so omega can see the division.
This splits ↔ into two goals: (⇒) and (⇐).
`t1 <;> t2` runs t2 on every goal that t1 produced. Here `intro h` moves the assumption of each implication into the context as h.

proof_steps.math: Since ⌊x/q⌋ ≥ 5 ⇔ x ≥ 5q, the condition is 10^7 ≤ 240dt + 10^6, i.e. 240dt ≥ 9·10^6, i.e. dt ≥ 37 500.
proof_steps.note: omega decides linear arithmetic over ℕ and ℤ, including `/` and `%` by numeric literals. It closes both directions in one call.

lessons.gotcha: omega can handle `/` here only because the divisor 2000000 is a literal. If the divisor were a variable, say `(dt * 240 + c) / d`, the problem would no longer be linear arithmetic and omega would fail. The project fixes its constants for this reason.

exercise.prompt: Translate into Lean and prove: ∀ n ∈ ℕ: 2 ≤ ⌊n/3⌋ ⇔ 6 ≤ n.
exercise.answer: `theorem third_ge2_iff (n : Nat) : 2 ≤ n / 3 ↔ 6 ≤ n := by constructor <;> intro h <;> omega`. It is proved in StudyA.lean; no ⌊⌋ is needed because Nat `/` already floors.

lessons.title: A count, i.e. a sum over a list: countAbove
lessons.why: The frame metrics count long frames (more than 34 ms, more than 50 ms). In math that is #{i : x_i > t}, or a sum of Iverson brackets. Without Mathlib there is no Finset or ∑ notation, so Lean writes it as filter, then length.
lessons.english: countAbove(t, xs) is the number of frames in the list that are strictly longer than t µs, with repeats counted.
lessons.math_latex: \forall t \in \mathbb{N},\ \forall xs = [x_1, \dots, x_n] \in \mathbb{N}^{*}:\quad \operatorname{countAbove}(t, xs) = \#\{\, i : x_i > t \,\} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} [\,x_i > t\,]
lessons.lean_excerpt: def countAbove (t : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Nat := (xs.filter (fun x => decide (t < x))).length

pairs.lean: def countAbove (t : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Nat
pairs.note: A function of two arguments has the type `Nat → List Nat → Nat`, one arrow per argument (this is called currying). You call it as `countAbove 10 [11, 11, 10, 5]`.
A finite sequence that keeps its order and its repeats. Frames that happen to have equal durations must each be counted, so a set would be the wrong model.
An anonymous function, written λx in math. You can also write `fun x ↦ ...`.

`x > t` is defined as `t < x` (`GT.gt` is a reducible definition, so the two are equal by `rfl`, although `rw` treats them as different terms). The library states its lemmas with < and ≤, so the project writes them that way.
`filter` needs a Bool test that it can compute. `decide` turns a decidable Prop into true or false.
This keeps the elements that pass the test, in their original order. Dot notation `xs.filter p` is short for `List.filter p xs`.
The size of the filtered list. `#eval [11, 11, 10, 5].filter (fun x => decide (10 < x))` gives `[11, 11]`, which has length 2.

pairs.lean: (xs.map (fun x => if t < x then 1 else 0)).sum
pairs.note: The literal Σ form uses map, then List.sum. StudyA.lean proves the two forms equal (countAbove_eq_sum) by induction on the list.

lessons.gotcha: `List` is not a set. It keeps duplicates and order, which is exactly why a count like #{i : …} over indices is right here. The project avoids Mathlib, so there is no `Finset` and no `∑ x ∈ s, f x` notation. Sums and counts are built from `filter`, `map`, `length`, `sum` or `foldl`, and facts about them are proved by `induction xs`.

exercise.prompt: Write countAtMost(t, xs) = #{i : x_i ≤ t} in Lean, in the same style as countAbove. Then state that the two counts add up to the length of the list.
exercise.answer: `def countAtMost (t : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : Nat := (xs.filter (fun x => decide (x ≤ t))).length`, and `theorem countAbove_add_countAtMost (t : Nat) (xs : List Nat) : countAbove t xs + countAtMost t xs = xs.length`. Both are in StudyA.lean and the theorem is proved by induction on xs.

lessons.title: Bool (computed) versus Prop (stated): onTime_of_le
lessons.why: The project's decision functions return a Bool so that the program can run them. The theorems talk about Props. Every spec has to cross between the two, and `decide` with `= true` is that crossing.
lessons.english: If work a is componentwise at most work b and b fits the frame budget, then a fits the budget too.
lessons.math_latex: \forall u \in \mathbb{N}^{3},\ \forall B \in \mathbb{N},\ \forall a, b \in \mathbb{N}^{4}:\quad a \preceq b \ \land\ \operatorname{onTime}(u, B, b) \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{onTime}(u, B, a)
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem onTime_of_le (u : UnitCost) (budgetUs : Nat) {a b : Work} (h : a.le b)
    (hb : onTime u budgetUs b = true) : onTime u budgetUs a = true := by
  simp only [onTime, decide_eq_true_eq] at *
  exact Nat.le_trans (mainUs_mono u h) hb

pairs.note: A triple of numbers is a `structure` with named fields: u.style, u.layout, u.paint. A concrete value can be written with angle brackets, `⟨1, 1, 1⟩`.
Lean names can be descriptive; B and budgetUs play the same role.
These are implicit, because h and hb already mention a and b.
`a.le b` is `Work.le a b`, called with dot notation. Its definition (Cost.lean:45) is a Prop made of four ≤ joined by ∧: `a.scriptUs ≤ b.scriptUs ∧ ...`.
"A ∧ B ⇒ C" is written as two separate hypotheses. A → B → C means the same thing and is more convenient to use.

pairs.lean: def onTime ... : Bool := decide (mainUs u w ≤ budgetUs)
pairs.note: This is Cost.lean:89. onTime computes a Bool. `decide` turns the Prop mainUs u w ≤ B into true or false.
To use a Bool as a statement, you compare it with `true`, the lowercase Bool value. The capitalised `True` is the Prop that always holds, which is a different thing.
The conclusion has the same shape: the computed test gives true on a.

proof_steps.math: Unfolding onTime, the hypothesis says mainUs(u, b) ≤ B, and we must show mainUs(u, a) ≤ B.
proof_steps.note: `decide_eq_true_eq : (decide p = true) = p` is the bridge from Bool back to Prop. `at *` rewrites every hypothesis and the goal.

proof_steps.math: By monotonicity mainUs(u, a) ≤ mainUs(u, b), and mainUs(u, b) ≤ B, so by transitivity mainUs(u, a) ≤ B.
proof_steps.note: `mainUs_mono u h` is the earlier theorem (Cost.lean:59) applied to h. `Nat.le_trans : x ≤ y → y ≤ z → x ≤ z` chains the two inequalities.

lessons.gotcha: Bool and Prop are different. `true`/`false` are Bool values that a program computes. `True`/`False` and `n ≤ B` are Props that a proof establishes. When a Bool b appears where a Prop is expected, Lean quietly rewrites it to `b = true`. Writing `= True` instead gives a confusing double coercion: `fits n B = True` elaborates to `(fits n B = true) = True`.

exercise.prompt: With `def fits (n B : Nat) : Bool := decide (n ≤ B)`, which statement says fits(n, B) = true ⇔ n ≤ B?  (A) `fits n B ↔ n ≤ B`  (B) `fits n B = true ↔ n ≤ B`  (C) `fits n B = True ↔ n ≤ B`
exercise.answer: B is the clear form, and `by simp [fits]` proves it (fits_iff in StudyA.lean). A elaborates to exactly B, because Lean coerces a Bool used as a Prop to `_ = true`. C also elaborates, but to `(fits n B = true) = True ↔ n ≤ B`, which is not what was meant, so avoid it. `#check @fits_iff_A` and `#check @fits_iff_C` in StudyA.lean show both elaborations.

lessons.title: Truncated subtraction on ℕ: countAbove34_sub_tick5
lessons.why: This theorem shows that the old ">34 ms" count and the new "≥ 5 ticks" count differ by exactly the frames in the 34.0-37.5 ms band. It contains a subtraction on ℕ, which is a classic Lean trap.
lessons.english: The number of frames over 34 000 µs, minus the number of frames of at least 5 ticks, equals the number of frames in the range 34 000 < x ≤ 37 499 µs.
lessons.math_latex: \forall xs = [x_1, \dots, x_n] \in \mathbb{N}^{*}:\quad \operatorname{countAbove}(34\,000, xs) \mathbin{\dot-} \#\{\, i : 5 \le \operatorname{tick}(x_i) \,\} = \#\{\, i : 34\,000 < x_i \le 37\,499 \,\}
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem countAbove34_sub_tick5 (xs : List Nat) :
    countAbove 34000 xs - (xs.filter (5 ≤ tick ·)).length
      = (xs.filter (fun x => 34000 < x ∧ x ≤ 37499)).length := by
  induction xs with
  | nil => simp [countAbove]
  | cons x xs ih =>
    have hk := tick_ge5_iff x
    have hle : (xs.filter (5 ≤ tick ·)).length ≤ countAbove 34000 xs := by
      rw [tick5_eq_countAbove]; exact countAbove_antitone (by omega) xs
    simp only [countAbove] at hle ih ⊢
    rw [List.filter_cons, List.filter_cons, List.filter_cons]
    split <;> split <;> split <;> simp_all [List.length_cons] <;> omega

pairs.note: The statement quantifies over every list of frame durations, including the empty list.
This reuses the def from lesson A4.
On Nat, `-` is truncated subtraction (monus): a - b = 0 whenever b > a. The docstring writes ∸ so that the math says exactly what Lean means.
`(5 ≤ tick ·)` is short for `fun x => 5 ≤ tick x`; the dot `·` marks the hole. It is a Prop-valued function, and Lean inserts `decide` automatically (`#check` shows `decide (5 ≤ tick x)`).
Math's chained inequality must be split into two comparisons joined by ∧. Lean has no a < x ≤ b chains.
An equation between two Nat values, and it holds for every list. Each side is the length of a filtered list.

proof_steps.math: We argue by induction on the list xs.
proof_steps.note: This makes two cases, matching how a List is built: `nil` is the empty list, and `cons x xs` is the list with head x and tail xs.

proof_steps.math: Base case: for the empty list both sides are 0.
proof_steps.note: `simp` evaluates filter and length on [], which leaves 0 - 0 = 0.

proof_steps.math: Step: assume the claim for xs (call it ih) and prove it for x :: xs.
proof_steps.note: `ih` is the induction hypothesis, stated for the tail xs.
This puts lesson A3's iff, applied to the head x, into the context so the later automation can use it.

proof_steps.lean:
have hle : (xs.filter (5 ≤ tick ·)).length ≤ countAbove 34000 xs := by
      rw [tick5_eq_countAbove]; exact countAbove_antitone (by omega) xs
proof_steps.math: On the tail, the ≥5-tick count equals countAbove(37 499, ·), which is at most countAbove(34 000, ·) because a higher threshold never counts more. So the subtraction never truncates.
proof_steps.note: This is the key step for ∸. omega understands truncated subtraction exactly: it case-splits on b ≤ a versus a < b. Without hle, though, the truncating case is a genuine counter-model of the step (ih alone does not rule out countAbove 34000 xs < the ≥5-tick count). hle removes that case. `rw` rewrites using tick5_eq_countAbove, and `countAbove_antitone` needs 34000 ≤ 37499, which `by omega` proves.

proof_steps.math: Write every count in its filter-length form.
proof_steps.note: `⊢` stands for the goal, so this unfolds countAbove in hle, in ih and in the goal.

proof_steps.math: For each of the three filters, the head x either passes the test (the count goes up by 1) or it does not.
proof_steps.note: `List.filter_cons` turns `filter p (x :: xs)` into `if p x then x :: filter p xs else filter p xs`. It is applied once for each of the three filters.

proof_steps.math: Check all 2·2·2 cases. In each one the lengths change by 0 or 1, and the equation follows from ih, hle and hk by arithmetic.
proof_steps.note: Each `split` case-splits one `if`. `simp_all` simplifies the lengths, and together with omega (using hk) it closes the impossible cases, for example 5 ≤ tick x with x ≤ 34 000.

lessons.gotcha: Subtraction on ℕ truncates: `(3 : Nat) - 5 = 0`, not -2. Identities like (a - b) + b = a are false without the side condition b ≤ a, and a proof that needs a - b to behave like ordinary subtraction must have b ≤ a available (omega splits ∸ into both cases and needs the bound to rule out the truncating one). That is why the proof first establishes hle. On `Int`, `3 - 5 = -2` and the identity holds unconditionally.

exercise.prompt: Is `theorem t (a b : Nat) : a - b + b = a` provable? If not, give a counterexample and fix the statement.
exercise.answer: No. With a = 0, b = 1 you get (0 - 1) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1 ≠ 0. StudyA.lean proves `sub_add_counterexample : (0 : Nat) - 1 + 1 ≠ 0 := by decide`. The fix adds the side condition: `theorem sub_add_of_le {a b : Nat} (h : b ≤ a) : a - b + b = a := by omega`. On Int no hypothesis is needed: `theorem int_sub_add (a b : Int) : a - b + b = a := by omega`.

lessons.title: Dominance: more work never costs less (mainUs_mono)
lessons.why: This is the screening theorem of the cost model. If a variant's per-frame work is no larger than the base's in every component, it cannot cost more main-thread time on any device, whatever the unit costs are. So no calibration is needed to rule it in.
lessons.english: For any non-negative unit costs, if work a is at most work b in each of the four counts, then a's main-thread time is at most b's.
lessons.math_latex: \forall u \in \mathbb{N}^{3},\ \forall a, b \in \mathbb{N}^{4}:\quad a \preceq b \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{mainUs}(u, a) \le \operatorname{mainUs}(u, b), \qquad \operatorname{mainUs}(u, w) = s + u_{\mathrm{style}}\, e + u_{\mathrm{layout}}\, \ell + u_{\mathrm{paint}}\, k
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem mainUs_mono (u : UnitCost) {a b : Work} (h : a.le b) : mainUs u a ≤ mainUs u b := by
  obtain ⟨h1, h2, h3, h4⟩ := h
  unfold mainUs
  have := Nat.mul_le_mul_left u.style h2
  have := Nat.mul_le_mul_left u.layout h3
  have := Nat.mul_le_mul_left u.paint h4
  omega

pairs.note: An explicit binder. UnitCost is a structure with three Nat fields, so u is a point of N^3. The condition 'c >= 0' never appears because a Nat cannot be negative.
Curly braces make these arguments implicit. Lean works out a and b from the type of h, so a caller writes `mainUs_mono u h` and never passes a or b.
The premise of the implication becomes a named argument: a proof h of `a ⪯ b`. `a.le b` is dot notation for `Work.le a b`, which is defined as a chain of four ≤ joined by ∧.
Function application is written by juxtaposition, with no parentheses or commas. The function is curried, taking one argument after another.
This is ≤ on Nat. It is a Prop (a statement), not a Bool, so a theorem can claim it.
Subscripts become field access; the product u_style·e appears as `u.style * w.styleElems` inside the unfolded mainUs.

pairs.math: e_a \le e_b \Rightarrow u_{\mathrm{style}}\, e_a \le u_{\mathrm{style}}\, e_b
pairs.note: This is a core library lemma: k * m ≤ k * n follows from m ≤ n. On Nat it needs no hypothesis 0 ≤ k.

proof_steps.math: Write a ⪯ b out as s_a ≤ s_b, e_a ≤ e_b, ℓ_a ≤ ℓ_b and k_a ≤ k_b.
proof_steps.note: h has type `A ∧ (B ∧ (C ∧ D))` (∧ nests to the right). The pattern ⟨…⟩ destructures all three ∧ at once into four hypotheses.

proof_steps.math: Expand both costs: we must show s_a + u_s e_a + u_l ℓ_a + u_p k_a ≤ s_b + u_s e_b + u_l ℓ_b + u_p k_b.
proof_steps.note: This replaces the defined name with its body in the goal.

proof_steps.math: Since u_style ≥ 0, e_a ≤ e_b gives u_style·e_a ≤ u_style·e_b.
proof_steps.note: This adds an anonymous hypothesis `this` to the context. Lean checks that h2 has exactly the type the lemma expects.
This is a second anonymous fact. The earlier `this` is shadowed but still visible to omega.
This is the third scaled inequality.

omega decides linear arithmetic over ℕ and ℤ. It treats `u.style * w.styleElems` as an opaque atom because it cannot multiply two variables. That is why the three `have` lines supply the scaled inequalities first.

lessons.gotcha: Non-negativity lives in the type: the costs are ℕ, so 'for every c ≥ 0' costs nothing to state. Port the formula to ℤ and the same statement becomes false: unit cost −1 plus one more element gives a lower cost (StudyB `B1_int_needs_nonneg`, proved by decide). The converse also fails: mainUs maps the four counts to one number, so equal or lower cost says nothing about each component (e.g. all unit costs 0).

exercise.prompt: Translate to Lean: 'It is not true that for all unit costs u and works a, b, mainUs(u,a) ≤ mainUs(u,b) implies a ⪯ b.' Is it true?
exercise.answer: `¬ ∀ (u : UnitCost) (a b : Work), mainUs u a ≤ mainUs u b → a.le b`. It is true. Take u = (0,0,0), a = (0,1,0,0) and b = (0,0,0,0). Both costs are 0, so 0 ≤ 0, but e_a = 1 > 0 = e_b. Proved as `B1_converse_false` in StudyB.lean.

lessons.title: A flag override changes exactly one part (override_diff)
lessons.why: This is the A/B isolation rule for feature flags. A variant built by overriding one part differs from its control in exactly that part, and this holds by construction, so it never needs a runtime check.
lessons.english: If configuration c does not already give part p the variant v, then c and c with p overridden to v differ in exactly the list [p].
lessons.math_latex: \forall c \in \mathrm{Config},\ p \in \mathrm{Part},\ v \in \mathrm{Variant}:\quad c(p) \ne v \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{diff}\big(c,\ c[p \mapsto v]\big) = [p]
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem override_diff (c : Config) (p : Part) (v : Variant) (h : c p ≠ v) :
    diff c (override c p v) = [p] := by
  cases p <;> simp [diff, override, Part.all, h]

pairs.note: Config is an abbreviation for `Part → Variant`. A configuration is literally a total function, so `c p` is function application.
Part is an inductive type with six named constructors (a finite set listed by name), so `cases p` produces exactly six concrete goals, one per part.
Variant is an abbreviation for String.
The premise is a named argument. ≠ is the Prop `¬ (c p = v)`.
Function update, defined as `fun q => if q = p then v else c q`. The `if q = p` needs decidable equality on Part, which the `deriving DecidableEq` clause provides.
diff is a list comprehension: `Part.all.filter (fun q => a q != b q)`. It is a list in a fixed order, not a set, because there is no Mathlib Finset here.
This is equality of lists. It says more than the set equality {p}, because it also rules out duplicates and fixes the order.

proof_steps.lean: cases p <;> simp [diff, override, Part.all, h]
proof_steps.math: Check the six parts one by one. Unfold the definitions: every other part q has c(q) = c(q) and drops out of the filter, while part p has c(p) ≠ v and stays.
proof_steps.note: `cases p` creates six goals, one per constructor. `<;>` runs simp on each of them. simp needs a concrete p to decide each `if q = p` in the six-element list. It uses h for the one comparison it cannot compute.

lessons.gotcha: Bool versus Prop. The hypothesis uses ≠, which is a Prop. diff filters with `!=` (bne), which returns a Bool. They mean the same thing, but they are different terms, and simp's bne/≠ lemmas are what connect them. Second trap: without `cases p`, simp cannot evaluate `if q = p` for a variable p and gets stuck.

exercise.prompt: Translate and prove: overriding a part with the value it already has changes nothing, i.e. ∀ c, p: diff(c, c[p ↦ c(p)]) = [ ].
exercise.answer: `theorem B2_override_same (c : Config) (p : Part) : diff c (override c p (c p)) = [] := by cases p <;> simp [diff, override, Part.all]` (in StudyB.lean). No hypothesis is needed because the new value is c p itself.

lessons.title: 'Better' is sound when higher is better (better_sound_higher)
lessons.why: When the loop records 'better' for an fps-style metric, every variant run really was strictly higher than every control run. The proof reuses the lower-is-better result through a negation duality instead of repeating the case analysis.
lessons.english: If the higher-is-better verdict says better, then every variant run is strictly greater than every control run.
lessons.math_latex: \forall C, V \in \mathbb{Z}^{*}:\quad \operatorname{verdict}(\mathrm{higher}, C, V) = \mathrm{better} \;\Rightarrow\; \forall y \in V,\ \forall x \in C:\ x < y
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem better_sound_higher {ctl var : List Int} (h : verdict .higher ctl var = .better) :
    ∀ y ∈ var, ∀ x ∈ ctl, x < y := by
  rw [verdict_higher_eq_lower_neg] at h
  intro y hy x hx
  have := better_sound h (-y) (List.mem_map.mpr ⟨y, hy, rfl⟩) (-x) (List.mem_map.mpr ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩)
  omega

pairs.note: ℤ* (finite sequences of integers) becomes List Int, which keeps repeats and order. The arguments are implicit because Lean reads them off h.
`.higher` is short for `Dir.higher`. The leading dot tells Lean to look the name up in the expected type. The premise of ⇒ becomes the argument h.
A bounded quantifier: sugar for `∀ y, y ∈ var → …`. #check prints the expanded form.
Strict < on Int, so ties are excluded. The swapped `y < x` would also typecheck, which is why the direction matters.
Inside verdict_higher_eq_lower_neg, `(- ·)` is shorthand for `fun x => -x`, and List.map applies it to every element.
Membership in a mapped list is an existential: `b ∈ l.map f ↔ ∃ a, a ∈ l ∧ f a = b`. `.mpr` uses the ← direction with witness y, proof hy and `rfl` for -y = -y.
A theorem is a function. Applying it to h, a point and a membership proof instantiates its ∀ binders in order.

proof_steps.math: By duality, verdict(higher, C, V) = verdict(lower, −C, −V), so the latter is 'better'.
proof_steps.note: This rewrites the hypothesis h with a proved equation (left side to right side).

proof_steps.math: Let y ∈ V and x ∈ C.
proof_steps.note: This introduces the four binders of `∀ y, y ∈ var → ∀ x, x ∈ ctl → …`. hy and hx are the membership proofs.

proof_steps.lean: have := better_sound h (-y) (List.mem_map.mpr ⟨y, hy, rfl⟩) (-x) (List.mem_map.mpr ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩)
proof_steps.math: Lower-is-better soundness, applied to −y ∈ −V and −x ∈ −C, gives −y < −x.
proof_steps.note: Lean checks that each membership proof matches the mapped lists from the rewritten h.
omega derives x < y from −y < −x by integer linear arithmetic.

lessons.gotcha: The duality needs ℤ. ℕ has no negation, and the nearest substitute `0 - x` truncates to 0, so all values would collapse (`#eval` in StudyB prints [0, 0, 0]). That is one reason the verdict's values are Int even though frame counts and µs are never negative.

exercise.prompt: Translate and prove: under lower-is-better, verdict = worse ⇒ ∀ x ∈ C, ∀ y ∈ V: x < y.
exercise.answer: `theorem B3_worse_sound {ctl var : List Int} (h : verdict .lower ctl var = .worse) : ∀ x ∈ ctl, ∀ y ∈ var, x < y`. Proof: `unfold verdict at h; split at h; · cases h; · simp only at h; split at h; · cases h; · split at h; · exact (below_spec _ _).mp ‹_›; · cases h` (see StudyB.lean for the layout). Each `cases h` closes a branch where h says, for example, `.better = .worse`, which is impossible.

lessons.title: The A/B verdict and its 1/70 false-win rate (verdict)
lessons.why: This is the loop's landing rule. Its false-win rate under 'no real difference' is 1 in C(8,4) = 70 for 4 vs 4 runs, about 1.4 %. That rate decides how many comparisons per experiment are safe.
lessons.english: With at least 3 runs per side, lower-is-better calls the variant better only if every variant run is below every control run, worse in the mirror case, and noise otherwise. With 4 vs 4 distinct ranks, exactly 1 of the 70 rank splits is 'better'.
lessons.math_latex: \begin{gathered} \operatorname{verdict}(\mathrm{lower}, C, V) = \begin{cases} \mathrm{tooFew} & \text{if } |C| < 3 \ \lor\ |V| < 3 \\ \mathrm{better} & \text{else if } \operatorname{below}(V, C) \\ \mathrm{worse} & \text{else if } \operatorname{below}(C, V) \\ \mathrm{noise} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\[1em] \operatorname{verdict}(\mathrm{higher}, C, V) = \begin{cases} \mathrm{tooFew} & \text{if } |C| < 3 \lor |V| < 3 \\ \mathrm{better} & \text{else if } \operatorname{below}(C, V) \\ \mathrm{worse} & \text{else if } \operatorname{below}(V, C) \\ \mathrm{noise} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\[1em] \frac{\#\{(C,V) \in \mathrm{splits} : \operatorname{verdict}(\mathrm{lower}, C, V) = \mathrm{better}\}}{|\mathrm{splits}|} = \frac{1}{\binom{8}{4}} = \frac{1}{70} \\ \text{(}= \Pr_{\text{null}}[\mathrm{better}]\text{ under the exchangeability assumption, which is not proved)} \end{gathered}
lessons.lean_excerpt:
def verdict (d : Dir) (ctl var : List Int) : Verdict :=
  if ctl.length < minRuns ∨ var.length < minRuns then .tooFew
  else match d with
    | .lower  => if below var ctl then .better else if below ctl var then .worse else .noise
    | .higher => if below ctl var then .better else if below var ctl then .worse else .noise

pairs.lean: def verdict (d : Dir) (ctl var : List Int) : Verdict :=
pairs.note: A def is a computable function. Lean rejects it unless every case returns a value (a total function). Verdict is a four-constructor inductive.
|·| is List.length, which counts repeats. ∨ is the Prop Or, and `if` on it works because < on Nat is decidable. minRuns is a def equal to 3.
A constructor of Verdict, written with the leading-dot shorthand.

pairs.lean: if … then … else if … then … else …
pairs.note: The nested if/else fixes the order of evaluation, which is what 'first match wins' means for overlapping conditions.
Pattern matching on Dir's two constructors. Lean checks the match is exhaustive.
`below b a` means every element of b is strictly below every element of a. It returns a Bool, and `if` on a Bool b means `if b = true`.
Theorem splits_length in StudyB.lean, proved by decide. There is no Mathlib binomial or Finset, so a hand-written `choose` lists the 4-subsets and `decide` counts them.

lessons.gotcha: Argument order is not checked by types. `below var ctl` and `below ctl var` both typecheck, and swapping them silently turns 'better' into 'worse'. Only the soundness theorems (better_sound, better_sound_higher) and the #guard examples catch that. Also, the 1/70 is a counting theorem plus a modelling assumption: under no real difference and no ties, the 70 rank splits are equally likely. Lean proves the count, not the exchangeability.

exercise.prompt: Write in Lean: 'of the 70 ways to give 4 of the ranks 1..8 to the variant, exactly one makes verdict(lower, C, V) = better, so p = 1/70 in ℚ'.
exercise.answer: In StudyB.lean: `def splits := (choose 4 ranks).map fun v => (ranks.filter (fun x => !v.contains x), v)`, `def wins := (splits.filter fun cv => verdict .lower cv.1 cv.2 == .better).length`, `theorem splits_length : splits.length = 70 := by decide`, `theorem wins_eq_one : wins = 1 := by decide`, `def falseBetterProb : Rat := (wins : Rat) / (splits.length : Rat)`, and `theorem falseBetterProb_eq : falseBetterProb = 1 / 70 := by unfold falseBetterProb; rw [wins_eq_one, splits_length]; rfl`. The only winning split gives the variant ranks [1,2,3,4].

lessons.title: Structural induction on a list (countAbove_antitone)
lessons.why: This guarantees gt54 ≤ gt50 ≤ gt46 on every run. Raising the jank threshold never raises the count, so the buckets are consistent by proof rather than by test.
lessons.english: For any list of frame times, raising the threshold from t to t' never increases the number of frames strictly above it.
lessons.math_latex: \forall t, t' \in \mathbb{N},\ \forall xs \in \mathbb{N}^{*}:\quad t \le t' \;\Rightarrow\; \operatorname{countAbove}(t', xs) \le \operatorname{countAbove}(t, xs), \qquad \operatorname{countAbove}(t, xs) = \#\{\, i : x_i > t \,\}
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem countAbove_antitone {t t' : Nat} (h : t ≤ t') (xs : List Nat) :
    countAbove t' xs ≤ countAbove t xs := by
  induction xs with
  | nil => simp [countAbove]
  | cons x xs ih =>
    simp only [countAbove, List.filter_cons] at *
    by_cases h1 : t' < x
    · have h2 : t < x := by omega
      simp [h1, h2]; omega
    · by_cases h2 : t < x
      · simp [h1, h2]; omega
      · simp [h1, h2]; omega

pairs.note: Implicit, because Lean infers them from h.
The premise is a named hypothesis.
Explicit and placed after h, so the type reads 't ≤ t' → ∀ xs, …', matching the English order.
Defined as `(xs.filter (fun x => decide (t < x))).length`. The count is filter followed by length, standing in for a Finset cardinality (no Mathlib).

pairs.lean:
induction xs with
  | nil => … | cons x xs ih =>
pairs.note: A list is either [] or x :: xs, and Lean creates one goal per constructor. In the cons case, ih is the claim for the tail xs.
x > t' is written t' < x. Lean prefers < and ≤ with the smaller side on the left.
Library equation: `filter p (x :: xs) = if p x = true then x :: filter p xs else filter p xs`.

proof_steps.note: Structural induction: one goal for [] and one for x :: xs.
simp unfolds countAbove, computes filter [] = [] and length 0, and closes 0 ≤ 0.

proof_steps.math: Let the list be x :: xs and assume the claim for xs.
proof_steps.note: ih : countAbove t' xs ≤ countAbove t xs.

proof_steps.math: Split each count into [x counted] plus the count of xs.
proof_steps.note: `at *` rewrites the goal and every hypothesis, ih included, so both use the same unfolded form.
Splits on a Prop. The second branch gets h1 : ¬ t' < x.

proof_steps.lean: · have h2 : t < x := by omega
proof_steps.math: Then x > t as well, since t ≤ t'.
proof_steps.note: omega combines h and h1.

proof_steps.math: Both counts go up by 1, so the goal reduces to the induction hypothesis.
proof_steps.note: simp resolves both ifs to their then-branches, so each length gains 1, and simp cancels the +1, leaving n′ ≤ n, which omega closes from ih.

proof_steps.math: Case 2: x ≤ t'. Subcase on whether x > t.
proof_steps.note: A nested case split.

proof_steps.math: x ≤ t' but x > t: only the right count goes up, n' ≤ n + 1.
proof_steps.note: omega uses ih.

proof_steps.math: x ≤ t: neither count changes, so ih is exactly the goal.
proof_steps.note: Both ifs resolve to their else-branches.

lessons.gotcha: filter needs a Bool predicate, so the Prop `t < x` is wrapped as `decide (t < x)`. simp can pick a branch of `if decide (t' < x) = true` only after it is handed h1 or ¬h1, which is why every branch passes [h1, h2]. Also note the < versus ≤ edge: a frame exactly equal to t is not counted.

exercise.prompt: Translate and prove: countAbove(t, xs ++ ys) = countAbove(t, xs) + countAbove(t, ys). Do you need induction?
exercise.answer: `theorem B5_countAbove_append (t : Nat) (xs ys : List Nat) : countAbove t (xs ++ ys) = countAbove t xs + countAbove t ys := by simp [countAbove, List.filter_append]` (StudyB.lean). No explicit induction is needed, because the library lemmas filter_append and length_append were already proved by induction.

lessons.title: The device-lease invariant survives every command (step_inv)
lessons.why: This is the exclusivity bug class from v1 (I-041, duplicate waiters, a holder that is also waiting), ruled out by proof. There is at most one holder by type, and this theorem shows every command keeps the queue clean.
lessons.english: If a lease state satisfies the invariant (no waiters when the device is free, nobody queued twice, the holder not also waiting), then the state after any single command satisfies it too.
lessons.math_latex: \forall s \in \mathrm{State},\ \forall c \in \mathrm{Cmd}:\quad \operatorname{Inv}(s) \Rightarrow \operatorname{Inv}\big(\mathrm{step}(s, c)_1\big), \quad \operatorname{Inv}(h, Q) \iff (h = \bot \Rightarrow Q = [\,]) \land \operatorname{nodup}(Q) \land (\forall l:\ h = l \Rightarrow l.\mathit{owner} \notin Q)
lessons.lean_excerpt:
theorem step_inv {s : State} (c : Cmd) (h : Inv s) : Inv (step s c).1 := by
  cases c with
  | acquire o now ttl =>
    simp only [step]
    split
    · split
      · exact ⟨fun _ => rfl, List.nodup_nil, by simp⟩
      · exact h
    · rename_i l hl
      split
      · exact h
      · split
        · exact h
        · rename_i hne hnq
          refine ⟨by simp [hl], ?_, ?_⟩
          · rw [List.nodup_append]
            refine ⟨h.nodup, by simp, ?_⟩
            intro a ha b hb
            simp only [List.mem_singleton] at hb
            subst hb
            intro e; subst e; exact hnq ha
          · intro l' hl'
            simp only [hl, Option.some.injEq] at hl'
            subst hl'
            have := h.not_both l hl
            simp only [List.mem_append, List.mem_singleton, not_or]
            exact ⟨this, hne⟩
  | renew o now ttl =>
    simp only [step]
    split
    · split
      · rename_i l hl _
        refine ⟨by simp, h.nodup, ?_⟩
        intro l' hl'
        simp only [Option.some.injEq] at hl'
        subst hl'
        have := h.not_both l hl
        simp_all
      · exact h
    · exact h
  | release o now ttl =>
    simp only [step]
    split
    · split
      · exact promote_inv h.nodup
      · rename_i l hl _
        refine ⟨by simp [hl], h.nodup.erase o, ?_⟩
        intro l' hl'
        simp only [hl, Option.some.injEq] at hl'
        subst hl'
        exact fun hm => h.not_both l hl (List.mem_of_mem_erase hm)
    · exact h
  | tick now ttl =>
    simp only [step]
    split
    · split
      · exact promote_inv h.nodup
      · exact h
    · exact h

pairs.note: Implicit, because Lean reads s off h. State is a structure with fields holder : Option Lease and queue : List Owner.
Explicit: Lean cannot guess which command is meant. Cmd has four constructors, which is why the proof begins with `cases c`.
Inv is a structure valued in Prop: a conjunction with named fields. `h.nodup` and `h.not_both` pull out single clauses.
step returns a pair (State × Reply), and `.1` is the first projection (#check shows `.fst`).
Injectivity of `some` (⊥ is `none`, a held lease is `some l`): simp uses it to turn `some l = some l'` into `l = l'`.
Library fact: Nodup (l₁ ++ l₂) holds iff Nodup l₁, Nodup l₂ and the two lists are disjoint.
`List.Nodup.erase`: removing an element keeps the list duplicate-free. Dot notation chains it onto the proof h.nodup.
The anonymous constructor ⟨…⟩ builds the structure. Each `?_` becomes a new goal to prove next.

proof_steps.math: Case on the command: acquire, renew, release, tick.
proof_steps.note: Four goals, one per Cmd constructor.
Names the constructor's fields.
Uses step's equation for this constructor. A `match s.holder` remains.

proof_steps.math: Case on the holder: free (⊥) or held (l).
proof_steps.note: Splits the match into goals.
Splits the if.

proof_steps.math: Q = [ ]: the new state is ((o, now+ttl), [ ]). The empty queue has no repeats and does not contain the holder.
proof_steps.note: Three clauses: [] = [] by rfl, nodup_nil, and simp for ∉ [].

proof_steps.math: Q ≠ [ ]: refused, the state is unchanged.
proof_steps.note: The goal is literally Inv s.

proof_steps.math: Held by some lease l, with hl: holder = l.
proof_steps.note: Names the inaccessible hypotheses that split created.

proof_steps.math: Otherwise l.owner ≠ o and o ∉ Q.
proof_steps.note: Names those two facts.

proof_steps.math: The new state is (l, Q ++ [o]). The device is held, so the first clause is vacuous; two clauses remain.
proof_steps.note: The first field is closed by simp, since some l ≠ none.

proof_steps.math: Q ++ [o] has no repeats iff Q has none, [o] has none, and they are disjoint.
Q by the invariant, and [o] trivially; disjointness remains.

proof_steps.note: Eliminates the equation.

proof_steps.lean: intro e; subst e; exact hnq ha
proof_steps.math: If a = o then o ∈ Q, contradicting o ∉ Q.
proof_steps.note: Disjointness is stated as a ≠ b, so `intro e` assumes a = b.

proof_steps.math: Holder clause: let l' be the new holder.
The holder is unchanged, so l = l'.
Show l.owner ∉ Q ++ [o], i.e. l.owner ∉ Q and l.owner ≠ o.
Name l and hl; the owner equality stays unnamed.
proof_steps.note: `_` skips a name.

proof_steps.math: The new state is (l', Q) with l' = (o, max(…)). The device is held and the queue is unchanged.
Let l' be the new holder.

proof_steps.note: simp_all simplifies every hypothesis and the goal together.

proof_steps.math: The holder releases: the new state is promote(now, ttl, Q), which satisfies Inv because Q has no repeats.
proof_steps.note: Uses a lemma proved earlier.

proof_steps.math: Someone else releases: name l and hl.
The new state is (l, Q ⊖ o). Still held, and removal keeps no-repeats.

proof_steps.lean: exact fun hm => h.not_both l hl (List.mem_of_mem_erase hm)
proof_steps.math: If l.owner ∈ Q ⊖ o then l.owner ∈ Q, contradicting the invariant.
proof_steps.note: ∉ means '∈ → False', so the proof is a function.

proof_steps.math: Expired: promote the head of the queue.

lessons.gotcha: `split` and `cases` introduce hypotheses with inaccessible names (shown as l✝, h✝). You must name them with `rename_i` in the order they were introduced (`_` skips one) before you can use them, so a reordered definition breaks the proof script, not the math. Also, this is a one-step theorem: Inv for every reachable state is a separate induction (gap G3).

exercise.prompt: Translate and prove: every state reached from s₀ = (⊥, [ ]) by any list of commands satisfies Inv, where run(s, cs) folds step over cs.
exercise.answer: `def run (s : State) (cs : List Cmd) : State := cs.foldl (fun s c => (step s c).1) s`; `theorem inv_run (cs : List Cmd) : ∀ s, Lease.Inv s → Lease.Inv (run s cs) := by induction cs with | nil => intro s h; exact h | cons c cs ih => intro s h; exact ih _ (step_inv c h)`; `theorem inv_reachable (cs : List Cmd) : Lease.Inv (run {} cs) := inv_run cs {} inv_init` (StudyB.lean). The `∀ s` must stay inside the induction, because the start state changes at each step.

notation.typed: Nat  (\N or \nat gives ℕ, but ℕ is Mathlib-only notation)
notation.note: Natural numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. Without Mathlib, `ℕ` is an unknown identifier, so the project writes Nat.
Integers. Subtraction is ordinary; `/` rounds so the remainder is non-negative, e.g. -7 / 2 = -4.
Rationals, built into core Lean 4.35. Stored as a reduced numerator and denominator; (1 : Rat) / 0 = 0.

notation.lean: ∀ x : Nat, P x   or   (x : Nat) before the colon
notation.note: Binders before the colon of a theorem are universally quantified.
Bounded quantifier over a list, as in Verdict.lean's below_spec.
Prove it by giving a witness and a proof, ⟨x, hx⟩; use it with `obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ := h`.
An implication is a function from proofs of A to proofs of B, which is why the same arrow is used for function types.
Two implications, accessed as `.mp` (⇒) and `.mpr` (⇐); prove with `constructor`.
Build with ⟨h1, h2⟩; take apart with h.1 and h.2, or `obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := h`.
Build with Or.inl or Or.inr; take apart with `cases h` or `rcases`.
Defined as P → False.
The Prop with no proof. A theorem with conclusion `: False` says that its hypotheses cannot all hold together.
a ≥ b is defined as b ≤ a (equal by rfl); library lemmas are stated with ≤.
x > t is defined as t < x (equal by rfl).
a ≠ b means ¬ (a = b).
Membership in a List, as in Part.mem_all.
Function application is juxtaposition, with no parentheses or commas.

notation.typed: fun x => e  (or fun x \mapsto e)
notation.note: An anonymous function (λ). `(5 ≤ tick ·)` is short for fun x => 5 ≤ tick x.
Marks the argument position inside parentheses, as in `(- ·)` or `(5 ≤ tick ·)`.
Multiplication must be explicit; `a b` would mean a applied to b.
Nat division floors, and a / 0 = 0.
Truncated: 3 - 5 = 0 on Nat. Use Int for ordinary subtraction.
An ordered list that keeps repeats. [] is the empty list; x :: xs puts x in front of xs.
The number of entries, repeats included.
Counting without Finset; p must return a Bool, which Lean supplies via decide.
Sums over a list. No ∑ notation without Mathlib.
Pairs, as in Flags.lean's `List (Part × Variant)`.
Anonymous constructor for a structure such as UnitCost ⟨1, 1, 1⟩; also used to build ∧ and ∃ proofs.
Bool values are computed; Props are proved. A Bool b used as a Prop means b = true.
Turns a decidable Prop into a Bool; the bridge back is `decide_eq_true_eq`. Turning it into 0/1 needs `if P then 1 else 0`.
Used for definitions, and also for supplying a proof after a theorem's statement.

notation.math: \text{from } A \land B \land C \text{ get } A, B, C
notation.note: Splits a nested ∧ (or ∃) hypothesis into its parts.
Decides linear (in)equalities over ℕ and ℤ. Treats a product of two variables as an opaque atom.
Runs tactic t₂ on every goal that t₁ produces.

notation.math: \text{by cases on the if/match in } h
notation.note: One goal per branch of an if or match in h.
Closes a goal whose hypothesis equates two different constructors.

notation.math: \text{a hypothesis of the needed type (by assumption)}
notation.note: Refers to whichever hypothesis has the needed type, without naming it.
cons, append, and the singleton list.

notation.lean: induction xs with | nil => … | cons x xs ih => …
notation.note: Structural induction. ih is the claim for the tail.
Componentwise order on Work, defined as a ∧ of four ≤.

notation.lean: fun q => if q = p then v else f q
notation.typed: fun q => if q = p then v else f q
notation.note: Function update. Needs DecidableEq on the domain.
`·` is a placeholder: (- ·) is fun x => -x.
An optional value, i.e. a type with a bottom element ⊥ added.
First component of a pair (printed as .fst).
List.Nodup is a Prop.
Removes the first occurrence of o.
Each ?_ becomes a new goal.

notation.math: \text{let } x = y \text{; replace } x \text{ by } y
notation.note: Eliminates a variable using an equation h : x = y.
Gives names to inaccessible hypotheses in the order they were introduced.
Core Lean's Rat (no Mathlib), with a coercion from Nat.
